findings.title: Asynchronous legacy writes are derived from the request context
findings.body: In Create, and similarly in Delete, Update, and DeleteCollection, the background goroutine creates a timeout context from the incoming request context. Request contexts are normally canceled when the HTTP handler returns, so the 10-second timeout does not make the legacy write independent. The legacy operation may be canceled immediately after the API response is sent, causing mode 3 to skip the intended asynchronous legacy write. A detached context, with logger/values copied, should be used instead.

findings.title: Legacy Create uses the original request object instead of the created object
findings.body: Mode3.Create passes the original obj to Legacy.Create after Storage.Create has returned created. Storage may assign name, UID, resourceVersion, annotations, or defaults, and created is the canonical object that unified storage accepted. Passing the original object, rather than a deep copy of created, can create a different object in legacy storage or cause concurrent use of a mutable object. This can make legacy storage diverge from unified storage.

findings.title: Legacy Update reuses the request UpdatedObjectInfo instead of the unified result
findings.body: Mode3.Update calls Storage.Update with objInfo and then asynchronously calls Legacy.Update with the same objInfo. Legacy.Update will normally evaluate objInfo against the legacy store's current object, so patches, strategic merges, or resource-version-dependent updates can produce a different result or fail. To keep legacy consistent, the legacy update should receive an UpdatedObjectInfo that returns the exact object returned by Storage.Update, preferably a deep copy.

findings.title: Unordered background goroutines can leave legacy storage inconsistent
findings.body: Each write operation starts an independent goroutine to write to legacy storage without sequencing, queueing, or per-resource locking. Rapid create/update/delete operations can be applied to legacy out of order, for example a legacy delete can run before a legacy create or an older update can overwrite a newer one. Because mode 3 keeps legacy as a fallback, this can resurrect deleted objects or leave stale data if legacy is later used.

findings.title: Delete does not attempt legacy deletion when unified delete returns NotFound
findings.body: DualWriterMode3.Delete returns immediately on any Storage.Delete error, including NotFound. The previous behavior tolerated NotFound from unified storage and still attempted to delete from legacy storage. With the new behavior, objects that are already absent from unified storage but still present in legacy cannot be cleaned through the API, leaving orphaned legacy data.

findings.title: Delete success metric uses the object name as the kind label
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, the successful storage-duration metric is recorded with name as the third argument, while other call sites pass options.Kind. This labels the metric with the object name instead of the resource kind, producing incorrect aggregations and potentially unbounded metric cardinality.

findings.title: Several mode 3 metrics record the wrong store
findings.body: When Storage.Create fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 45; when Storage.Update fails, recordLegacyDuration is called at line 129; and the asynchronous Legacy.DeleteCollection result is recorded with recordStorageDuration at line 166. These record the duration or error state of the wrong store, making mode 3 observability misleading.

findings.title: Background legacy writes are detached and untracked
findings.body: Mode 3 launches a new goroutine for every write with no wait group, queue, or shutdown coordination. Destroy can close Storage and Legacy while background writes are still running, which may cause failures or panics if the underlying stores are closed. There is also no backpressure, so a slow legacy backend can cause unbounded goroutine growth.

findings.title: Asynchronous legacy write failures are not logged
findings.body: The background create, update, delete, and delete-collection paths only record a metric when the legacy operation fails. They do not log the error or cause. Because these writes are asynchronous and can fail due to cancellation, timeouts, conflicts, or backend errors, operators will have no actionable logs to diagnose legacy divergence.

findings.title: Delete puts the base logger into the context instead of the enriched logger
findings.body: In DualWriterMode3.Delete, a logger is created with name, kind, and method fields, but the context is set with klog.NewContext(ctx, d.Log) instead of that enriched logger. Downstream code logging from the context will miss those fields, unlike the other mode 3 methods.

findings.title: Mode 3 unit tests do not synchronize or set expectations for async legacy calls
findings.body: Mode3 methods start goroutines that call LegacyStorage, but the unit tests neither wait for those goroutines nor assert whether legacy was called. For example, TestMode3_Delete calls Delete without setting a Legacy.Delete expectation, so the asynchronous call can hit the mock unexpectedly and race with test completion. Create and Update tests set legacy expectations but never verify them, so they can pass even if the asynchronous legacy write never happens.

findings.title: Mode 3 integration tests check legacy APIs synchronously despite asynchronous legacy writes
findings.body: The added mode 3 subtests run doPlaylistTests, which creates, updates, and deletes through the Kubernetes API and then immediately reads the legacy playlist API. In mode 3 the legacy write happens asynchronously, so these checks are racy. Without polling or retry for mode 3, the integration test can flake or hide failures where the legacy write never completes.
